raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 16-year-old male presented with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) associated with EBV infection. He had two healthy sisters, with no family history of consanguinity. At ages 3 and 6 years, he suffered fissured clavicle, rotula, and forearm fractures associated with traumatism. He also had allergies to penicillin, fava beans, and some fruits. At age 15, he developed a urinary tract infection.
He started at age 16 with fever, cytopenias, elevated triglycerides, and documented hemophagocytosis, for which he was treated with cyclosporine, dexamethasone, and etoposide. Soon after discharge, he was readmitted with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, and herpetic stomatitis.
Blood counts showed pancytopenia, with Hb 7.5g/dL, white blood cells 2,200 (down to 300), neutrophils 1500 (down to 200), lymphocytes 1,100 (down to 14), monocytes 100, and platelets 19,000-29,000/mm3. Ferritin 14,724-225,300 ng/ml. Serum IgM was marginally low, too: IgG 515-1,280 mg/dL (normal range for age 600-1600), IgM 38 (50-190), IgA 272 mg/dL (80-280). IgG1 766, IgG2 154, IgG3 28.3, IgG4 16.9mg/dl. Serum autoantibodies (anti-Ro/La, ANA, lupus anticoagulant), and serologies for HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, and brucellosis, were all negative. EBV serum antibodies VCA (IgG), EA, and EBNA were positive. PCR identified 2,580 copies/ml of EBV in serum, and up to 239,411 cp/ml in bone marrow. A bone marrow aspirate (BMA) was normocellular, with megaloblastic changes and active hemophagocytosis. A second BMA found hypocellularity, low megakaryocytes, and 8 hemophagocytes, with EBER diffusely positive in numerous cells.
In addition to the HLH-2004 protocol (etoposide, dexamethasone, cyclosporine) and high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin, the patient received treatment with blood transfusions and filgrastim. He was admitted to the intensive care unit and required mechanical ventilation, despite which he progressed to disseminated intravascular coagulation with multiorgan failure and perished. Given the rapid course of the disease, further immunologic studies could not be performed.
A post-mortem WES analysis revealed a very rare heterozygous missense variant, predicted as pathogenic and highly conserved, in exon 7 of 15 of NFAT5, c.1291A>T (p.Thr431Ser), in the DNA-binding domain RHD (Rel homology domain); gnomAD exomes allele count 1 (minor allele frequency MAF 3.99x10-6), SIFT 0.04, PolyPhen2 0.996, CADD Phred 24.6 (Minimum significance cutoff 3.3). GERP++ RS 4.85. MutPred Top5 features predict a loss of sheet (p=0.014) and gain of a loop (p=0.024). Unfortunately, after the patient's death, the family was not willing to undergo family segregation studies. ( Figure 6 ).
A table comparing blood counts and acute phase serum reactants of both patients can be found in  Supplementary Materials  as  Table S1 . Tables listing other interesting (rare and likely pathogenic) variants found in the exomes of both patients can be also found as  Tables S2  and  S3 .

subjective.chief_complaint: A 16-year-old male presented with fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, and herpetic stomatitis during an acute relapse of Epstein-Barr virus-associated hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 16-year-old boy initially presented with fever, cytopenias, hypertriglyceridemia, and bone marrow hemophagocytosis triggered by EBV infection, and was treated with the HLH-2004 protocol (dexamethasone, cyclosporine, etoposide). Shortly after discharge, he was readmitted with relapsed fever, hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, herpetic stomatitis, profound pancytopenia, and extreme hyperferritinemia (up to 225,300 ng/mL).
subjective.past_medical_history: Traumatic clavicle, patella, and forearm fractures at ages 3 and 6; urinary tract infection at age 15; allergies to penicillin, fava beans (favism), and certain fruits; two healthy sisters and non-consanguineous parents.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, oral candidiasis, herpetic stomatitis, and bleeding/cytopenic symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Febrile with hepatosplenomegaly, oral candidiasis, and herpetic stomatitis.
objective.routine_investigations: Profound pancytopenia: Hb 7.5 g/dL, WBC 2,200/mm3 dropping to 300/mm3 (neutrophils 1,500 down to 200/mm3, lymphocytes 1,100 down to 14/mm3, monocytes 100/mm3), platelets 19,000-29,000/mm3. Hypertriglyceridemia and extreme hyperferritinemia (14,724 rising to 225,300 ng/mL). Immunoglobulins: IgG 515-1,280 mg/dL (normal: 600-1,600), low IgM 38 mg/dL (50-190), IgA 272 mg/dL (80-280), IgG1 766, IgG2 154, IgG3 28.3, IgG4 16.9 mg/dL. Negative HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, and brucellosis serologies; positive EBV VCA-IgG, EA, and EBNA antibodies with serum EBV PCR of 2,580 copies/mL.
objective.advanced_workup: ANA, anti-Ro/La, and lupus anticoagulant negative. Bone marrow aspirate PCR detected up to 239,411 copies/mL of EBV DNA, and repeat bone marrow aspirate showed hypocellularity, decreased megakaryocytes, active hemophagocytosis, and diffuse EBER in situ hybridization positivity. Postmortem whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a rare, highly conserved pathogenic heterozygous missense variant in the Rel homology DNA-binding domain of NFAT5 (exon 7, c.1291A>T, p.Thr431Ser; CADD 24.6).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Fulminant EBV viremia/bone marrow infection (239,411 copies/mL, EBER+), bone marrow hemophagocytosis, ferritin of 225,300 ng/mL, negative Brucella/other infectious serologies, and postmortem WES identification of a heterozygous pathogenic NFAT5 missense mutation (c.1291A>T, p.Thr431Ser) confirmed fatal EBV-driven hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) associated with NFAT5 immunodeficiency. Despite HLH-2004 therapy (etoposide, dexamethasone, cyclosporine), high-dose IVIG, filgrastim, transfusions, and ICU mechanical ventilation, he died of disseminated intravascular coagulation and multiorgan failure.
